Testimony of Ana Hicks, Policy Director, Human Services
Governor's Office of Policy Innovation and the Future (GOPIF)
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs
Neither For Nor Against LD 2064
On behalf of GOPIF and the Department of Education
Representative Noonan Murphy, Senator Rafferty and members of the Joint Standing Committee on
Education and CulturalAffairs, my name is Ana Hicks, and I am a Policy Director for Human
Sen/ices in the Governor's Office of Policy Innovation and the Future (GOPIF) where I oversee the
work of the Governor's Children's Cabinet. I am here to testify neither for nor against LD 2064 on
behalf of GOPIF and the Department of Education.
The Governor's Office of Policy Innovation and the Future was established in 2019 by Governor
Mills to address critical, long-term issues facing Maine, by engaging state agencies, stakeholders and the public in the planning and implementation of innovative, data-driven policy solutions.
Public pre-k partnerships between School Administrative Units (SAUs) and licensed child care or Head Start programs have proven to be an important component of the state's efforts to expand public pre~k to more 4-year-olds throughout the state. Through these partnerships, schools
establish memorandums of understanding (MOUs) with Head Starts or licensed child care
programs to deliver public pre-k education to 4-year~olds in their communities as long as these community programs meet the requirements of Chapter 124. The children are dually enrolled in the school and the community program.
These partnerships support schools to overcome barriers that may exist to providing public pre-k. Many schools do not have the space to house public pre-k classrooms for some or all of the four-
year-olds in their communities. In addition, public pre-k partnerships ensure that working families
can access before and after school care, meaning their young children do not have to make
multiple transitions throughout the school day. importantly, public pre-k partnerships support a
community's early care and education infrastructure ensuring a stronger mixed delivery system for all children birth to age five.
Currently 45 SAUs provide public pre-k through a partnership with either a Head Start program, child care program or both. Thirty-two SAUs partner with Head Start programs only. Five SAUs partnerwith both a Head Start program and a child care program. Eight SAUs partnerwith child care programs only. However, the US Department of Agriculture regulations related to school meals at off-site locations are making partnerships more challenging to operate and establish. In addition, they are creating inequities for children who are receiving their pre-k education at child care programs and therefore cannot participate in Maine's no cost school meals program. Currently some SAUs are covering the full cost of these meals and many of these SUAs have
expressed that they are finding these costs to be untenable. In a handful of cases, the child care programs, which are already operating on razor thin margins, are picking up the cost of the meals that are not reimbursable through the Child and Adult Care Food Program and often shifting the
costs on to parents through higher fees. Lastly, SAUs who might be interested in entering into

partnerships to expand public pre-k are hesitant to consider partnerships because of the inability to be reimbursed for meals.
The grant program proposed by the Senate President seeks to address a real challenge faced by the
state. We are testifying neither for nor against because the grant program will require additional
state generalfunds to operate. In addition, we have some recommendations for changes to the
proposed grant program.
1. The grant program should be operated by the Child Nutrition Team at the Department of
Education, not the Children's Cabinet Early Childhood Advisory Council (CCECAC). The
CCECAC is a stakeholder advisory committee that does not have the capacity, the program
expertise or the authority to operate this type of program.
2. The proposal should include funding for two staff members on the Child Nutrition Team. One staff person will be responsible for managing the grant program and the second staff
person will ensure that programs are following nutritional guidance and program quality standards. These positions are necessaryfor implementation of the program proposed in
the bill.
3. The statutoiy language should refer to Title 20-A Section 6602 as a basis for developing the nutritional guidelines. The Department of Education should craft both the nutritional guidance and the grant program eligibility and requirements in consultation with the Office
of Child and Family Services at DHHS to align with the child care licensing rules. The grant program guidelines established by DOE and DH HS will need to explicitly require that the
process for delivering and reimbursing meals be clearly laid out in the MOU between the
SAU and licensed community program.
4. The exact cost per student should not be specified in statute. The cost per student should be based upon reimbursement levels provided through the National School Lunch Program, allowing for reimbursement for breakfast and lunch depending on the hours of operation of the program. In Chapter 124, policy stipulates that meals should not be more than 3 hours apart. In addition, the infrastructure grants should include transportation as an allowable expense.
5. Grant funding should be available for schools partnering with licensed child care programs in the deliveiy of early childhood special education services for preschool students. This
will include meals for three-year-olds with an IEP who are enrolled in a school's special
education program and are receiving sen/ices in a licensed child care program. Enrollment in these partnerships will fluctuate from year to year for schools depending upon the
number of children with iEPs. Forthat reason, we recommend that the grant program use
the April 1 student counts as an estimate for future costs for programs.
We thank you for the opportunity to testify and provide recommendations for addressing this policy
challenge.
I am happy to answer any questions.
10059729:
Testimony in Support of LD 2064 An Act to Expand Access to Early Childhood Nutrition by Establishing a Grant Program for Public Preschools
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and Honorable Members of the Health and Human Services
Committee
February 5, 2026
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and Honorable Members of the Committee:
My name is Christine Frost-Bertinet, and I am the Assistant Superintendent for RSU 14, which serves the communities of Windham and Raymond. I am writing today to express my strong support for LD 2064: An Act to Expand Access to Early Childhood Nutrition by Establishing a Grant Program for Public Preschools.
In RSU 14, we have worked diligently to develop a high-quality mixed delivery public pre-kindergarten model that meets the diverse needs of our families. This model allows us to expand access to pre-k by partnering with three local community-based early childhood programs, enabling us to serve more children than our district buildings alone could accommodate. We are proud of this collaborative approach, and it has proven successful in providing excellent early learning experiences for our youngest students.
However, we face a significant and troubling inequity: the children enrolled in our public pre-k program who attend classes at our partner sites cannot receive school meals, while those attending pre-k in our district buildings can. This disparity exists not because we lack the capacity or willingness to serve these children, but solely because federal regulations prohibit us from doing so. Our school nutrition program is well-equipped and ready to deliver our outstanding breakfasts and lunches to our partner sites. We have the infrastructure, the expertise, and the commitment to ensure that every public pre-k student has access to nutritious meals, regardless of where their classroom is located.
This regulatory barrier creates an unjust two-tiered system within our own pre-k program. Young children attending public pre-k programs, taught by equally qualified and certified teachers, receive vastly different support simply based on their classroom location. For families already navigating food insecurity, this gap can be devastating. Early childhood nutrition is not merely a convenience; it is foundational to learning, development, and lifelong health.
LD 2064 offers a practical, commonsense solution. By establishing a grant program to support public preschools in providing meals to students at partner sites, this legislation would eliminate the inequity we currently face and ensure that all public pre-k students have equal access to nutrition. It would allow districts like RSU 14 to fully support our mixed delivery models and serve all children equitably.
Our communities have invested significantly in early childhood education because we understand its transformative impact. It is both unjust and illogical to exclude some of our most vulnerable students from the nutritional support they need to thrive simply because of where they sit during the school day.

I urge this committee to support LD 2064 and help us close this gap. Every public pre-k student in Maine deserves access to healthy meals, and this bill will make that possible.
Thank you for your time and consideration. I am happy to answer any questions you may have.
Respectfully submitted,
Christine Frost-Bertinet Assistant Superintendent RSU 14 (Windham and Raymond)

CCECAC letter re LD2064
February 5, 2026
Senator Rafferty, Chair Representative Murphy, Chair Members, Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs 100 State House Station Augusta, ME 04333-0100
Re: LD 2064, An Act to Expand Access to Early Childhood Nutrition by Establishing a Grant Program for Public Preschools
On behalf of the Children's Cabinet Early Childhood Advisory Council (CCECAC) we are pleased to write today to express our support of LD 2064, An Act to Expand Access to Early Childhood Nutrition by Establishing a Grant Program for Public Preschool.
The CCECAC is a legislatively-established Council that focuses on the implementation of early childhood policy and programming and serves as the State Advisory Council on Early Childhood Education and Care. The Council advises the Children's Cabinet and policymakers on a range of issues related to early childhood and works to ensure statewide coordination and collaboration among the wide range of early childhood programs and services in the State, including child care, Head Start, IDEA preschool and infants and families' programs, and pre-kindergarten programs and services. Its members include legislators, parents, child care providers, philanthropy, business and organizations that advance the well-being of children.
Members of the Council have long been concerned about the inequities posed by the current system for meals in public pre-k partnerships located in off-site locations. In Maine right now, the children, who participate in a public pre-K program housed within a public elementary school, are able to access free food through the state's school meals program. For those children who are enrolled in a public pre-K partnership located at an off-site location such as a child care or Head Start Program , however, free school meals are not available. For children enrolled in a public pre-K partnership at an off-site location, such as a child care or Head Start program, free school meals are not eligible for reimbursement through the National School Lunch Program. In some cases, these meals are funded by the School Administrative Unit when local funding is made available. In a handful of cases, child care centers pick up the meal costs for children that are not eligible for the Child and Adult Care Food Program.
It is important to the CCECAC that all Maine children - wherever they live, and wherever they are receiving their public education - are able to access good, nutritious food to support their growth, learning and ability to thrive. In addition, the Council supports the establishment of public pre-K partnerships between schools and child care programs. A number of the participants in our monthly meetings represent child care programs who are involved in successful partnerships with schools and are providing quality pre-k education and programming to 4 year olds. The current policy hinders the ability of child care programs to partner with schools.
We do want to point out to the Committees, however, that while the CCECAC is currently written into the draft statutory language as the administrator of the program, it is not positioned to do so. As an advisory council, we have neither the capacity nor the authority to engage in such work and to take on such responsibilities. To be clear, we are very strongly in support of the proposed new grant program we are just not the entity to manage it.

CCECAC letter re LD2064
We would, of course, look forward to providing input as the program envisioned under the legislation is further developed. As the Children's Cabinet Early Childhood Advisory Council, we believe the experiences and insights of the members of this group could be invaluable to helping to create a program that will meet the needs of students, families and providers. Thank you. Sincerely,
Colleen J. Quint, Chair On behalf of the members of the Children's Cabinet Early Childhood Advisory Council
10059732:
Testimony in Support of LD 2064 An Act to Expand Access to Early Childhood Nutrition by Establishing a Grant Program for Public Preschools
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and Honorable Members of the Health and Human
Services Committee
2/5/2026
My name is Hannah Marshall, and I am the Director of Space to Thrive, providing a birth-through-five early childhood center and before and after school programs in Windham and Raymond communities. Thank you for the opportunity to speak in support of this bill.
Space to Thrive serves 24 public pre-K children through a partnership with RSU 14. We are proud to be part of Maine's mixed-delivery public pre-K system and to work closely with our local school district to provide high-quality early learning experiences for young children.
However, one of the most significant challenges we face is access to meals for the public pre-K children we serve.
Our program is located just down the road from the RSU 14 school. The district would love to transport free school meals--breakfast and lunch--to our site for the children enrolled in public pre-K. Unfortunately, federal child nutrition regulations prevent this kind of sharing of resources, even though the children are publicly funded and enrolled through the school district.
Because of these federal restrictions, and without a state solution to bridge the gap, our program's budget does not allow us to provide breakfast and lunch to our public pre-K children. We do our best to offer a small snack each day to support children's needs, but families are required to send meals from home.
This situation feels deeply inequitable. It exposes the fractures and silos in how we serve publicly funded children differently based solely on the setting in which their classroom happens to be located. A four-year-old attending a school-based pre-K classroom receives meals, while a four-year-old attending a community-based public pre-K partnership does not--even though both children are part of the same public education system.
A four-year-old deserves to eat, regardless of early childhood setting.
This proposed grant program would make a real and immediate difference for our program and the families we serve. It would give Space to Thrive the opportunity to provide breakfast and lunch to our public pre-K children, ensuring they are nourished, ready to learn, and supported equitably.
This bill does not replace federal programs--it thoughtfully addresses where federal regulations fall short. It recognizes the reality of mixed-delivery public pre-K and offers a flexible, practical solution that centers children's basic needs.

I urge you to support this bill and help ensure that all public pre-K children--no matter where they learn--have access to the food they need to thrive.
Thank you for your time and consideration.

My name is Heather Marden, and I am testifying today on behalf of the Maine Association for
the Education of Young Children (MaineAEYC) in strong support of LD 2064.

MaineAEYC represents early childhood educators, program leaders, and advocates across the
state who are committed to ensuring that all young children---regardless of zip code, age, or
setting--have access to high-quality early learning experiences. LD 2064 is a critical step toward
that goal by addressing a gap that many pre-K partnership `sites experience every day: access to nutritious meals for young children.

"
Public pre-K partnerships are a cornerstone of Maine's mixed~delivery system, bringing together school districts and community-based early childhood programs to expand access for
families. These partnerships allow children to learn in settings that are often closer to home
and deeply connected to their communities. However, while these sites are delivering on
educational standards and outcomes, many lack the resources to provide consistent, nutritious meals due to funding limitations or federal restrictions that prevent the sharing of school
nutrition services.

For a four-year-old child, nutrition is not separate from learning--~it is foundational to it. Hunger
affects attention, behavior, and social-emotional development. When children do not have
access to adequate meals during the school day, educators are left trying to teach while also
managing unmet basic needs. This is not an issue of program quality or commitment; it is a structural gap that LD 2064 directly and thoughtfully addresses.
This bill also makes a broader and important policy statement. As a state, we must do better at
looking at and providing policy for children from birth through age five as a whole system, rather than fragmenting supports by age, funding stream, or the physical space in which
children are served. When public pre-K dollars are spent on children, that investment should
not result in those same children having less access to essential resources simply because they are in a community-based setting rather than a school building.

By providing targeted grants to support nutrition at pre-K partnership sites, LD 2064 promotes equity across settings and reinforces the principle that public investments in children should result in comparable access to essential supports, regardless of the setting in which services are delivered. It recognizes community-based programs as essential partners in Maine's early
_
learning system and ensures they have the tools needed to meet children's full, holistic needs.
This investment also supports working families and the early childhood workforce. Parents depend on stable, nurturing environments where their children are cared for comprehensively. Educators and program staff work every day to support children's growth and development, often filling gaps created by fragmented systems. Aligning supports across birth through five
benefits not only children, but the adults who work hard in these critical roles.
LD 2064 takes an important step in making the case for a more aligned, equitable early
childhood system in Maine. I hope we can pass this legislation and continue the work across this Committee and the Health and Human Services Committee to better align supports, value,
and policy for all children from birth through age five.
On behalf of MaineAEYC and the early childhood community across the state, I urge you to vote ought to pass on LD 2064. Thank you for your time, your leadership, and your commitment to
Maine's youngest learners.
Respectfully submitted,
Heather Marden, Maine Association for the Education of Young Children

Before the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs Thursday, February 5, 2026
Good afternoon, Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and the esteemed Members of the
Education and Cultural Affairs Cormnittee. I am Senator Henry Ingwersen, and I proudly
represent Senate District 32, which includes Arundel, Biddeford, Dayton, Hollis, and Lyman.
Today, I offer testimony in strong support of President Daughtry's LD 2064, "An Act to
Expand Access to Early Childhood Nutrition by Establishing a Grant Program for Public
Preschools."
Last week, as the Senate chair of the Health and Human Services Committee, I was happy to
work on two of my child care-related bills: LD 1728 and LD 2066.
The first bill, LD 1728, would put` into Maine statute the federal child care subsidy rules that
change the cap on co-payments for participants in the Child Care Affordability Program from
10% to 7%. It would allow the Health and Human Services Department to further reduce or
waive these co-payments for families with a child with a disability, families experiencing homelessness and families with a foster child. The Department would have to post information related to co-payment amounts on its website. Finally, it would require the Department to issue subsidies based on enrollment, rather than attendance, encouraging more child care providers to participate in child subsidy programs without having to accept below-market rates for child care
services.
The second bill, LD 2066, seeks to build on a successful two-year pilot program, which has
demonstrated effective coordination with the Child Care Affordability Program. The bill would make the Child Care Employment Award a permanent component of Maine's child care subsidy system, along with the Child Care Affordability Program. As of September 2025, the program currently supports 511 Maine children from 313 working families. Without additional funding, 470 children from 312 families will remain on the waitlist.
While both of these bills invest in Maine's essential child care system and lower costs for working parents, they do not provide the full investment that our infants and toddlers deserve.
President Daught1y's bill, LD 2064, recognizes that mixed delivery Pre-K is key for the survival

of the child care system as a whole. The lower ratio makes it profitable enough to uplift infant and toddler care.
It's also a direct response -to persistent food insecurity in the state. Last fall, when the federal
government shut down and withheld SNAP benefits, I spearheaded a letter to the U.S. Secretary
of Agriculture Brooke Rollins, which President Daughtry signed, urging the Secretary to tap into
contingency funds and release SNAP benefits to the 170,000 Mainers -- including children -- who
u
rely on this support.
At the same time, I met with community members at Youth Full Maine and the York County Food Pantry. I attended meetings with the Council of Mayors and the York County Food
Council. But most importantly, during National School Lunch Week I served free school meals to students at Hollis School and Mildred L. Day School. While there, I spoke with District Nutrition Directors and nutrition staff, who assured me that the free school meal program is one
of the most successful legislative efforts in recent state history. They report that more kids are
eating school meals. This committee should feel proud that we were able to bring universal free
school meals into law -- and keep it there.
During the weeks of uncertainty surrounding SNAP, parents could breathe a little easier knowing
their children would receive nutritious meals at school. Thinking back on that time now, it is
clear to me that the state has to do more to take on food insecurity.
It's why I introduced LD 2004 this session. It seeks to open up the sources of ftmding of
nutrition incentive programs, like Maine Harvest Bucks, so that the dollars are not dependent on
federal match dollars. After all, if the federal dollars disappear, we cannot lose other sources of
funding -- allowing Mainers to go hungry.
With LD 2064, we can make a clear, strong commitment to feeding children when they are
developing, growing, and learning. Aside from being the right thing to do, we cannot feed their
minds unless we feed their bellies, too. And there are no do-overs: We either nurture children
during these critical years or we miss the opportunity forever.
I thank the Committee for its time, and I urge all of you to vote Ought to Pass on LD 2064.

Testimony of Representative Holly Eaton in Support of

Before the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy and distinguished members of the Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs, my name is Holly Eaton, and I proudly represent House District 15, which includes the communities of Deer Isle, Stonington, Brooklin, Tremont, Southwest Harbor, Frenchboro, Swan's Island, Isle au Haut, and Vinalhaven.
I am here today in support of LD 2064, An Act to Expand Access to Early Childhood Nutrition by Establishing a Grant Program for Public Preschools. I am proud to be a cosponsor of this bill, and I appreciate the opportunity to speak both as a legislator and as a parent who has lived the reality this bill seeks to address.
Right now, approximately 17 districts across Maine are operating off-site public pre-K programs, serving about 250 young students. These programs are an essential part of how many communities -- especially rural and coastal communities like mine -- deliver public education. But unlike classrooms located within school buildings, off-site programs often face barriers to providing meals. LD 2064 helps close that gap by giving schools the tools they need to ensure that children enrolled in public education have access to breakfast, lunch, and a snack during the school day.
I'm speaking today not just as a legislator, but as a single parent who has navigated these systems firsthand -- and not that long ago. When my children were younger, I received support through WIC and at times relied on SNAP benefits to help keep food on the table. My youngest child attended Head Start, which serves as our local public pre-K option, and I was deeply grateful that meals were provided at school during a time when I truly needed that additional support. Having that consistency didn't just help my child -- it helped stabilize our entire household. I know many parents across Maine are in similar positions right now, balancing work, childcare and rising costs, and policies like this recognize that when we support children's basic needs, we support families as well.

My name is Dr. Phil Potenziano, and I am Superintendent of Brunswick School Deparrment from Brunswick, Maine. I am writing to express support for LD 2064: An Act to Expand Access to Early Childhood Nutrition by Establishing a Grant Program for Public Preschools.

Federal child nutrition programs were designed around meals served on a school campus or directly by a school food authority. While this model works for many traditional settings, it does not reflect the reality of Maine's mixed-delivery public pre-K system.

Community-based public pre-K partnership sites often fall outside these federal structures, even when they are publicly funded and serving children who are enrolled in public schools. As a result, children attending off-site partnership programs are excluded from universal school meals--not because of need, but because of where their classroom happens to be located.

This creates a clear inequity. Two children enrolled in the same public pre-K system can have very different access to meals based solely on geography. Families and providers should not be required to navigate federal complexity to meet a child's most basic need: food. Hunger should never be a byproduct of system design.

Federal regulations also limit flexibility for local solutions. School administrative units often cannot easily extend meal service to partnership sites due to federal constraints, and community-based providers are not adequately funded to absorb the cost of food for children in public pre-K partnerships. These are structural barriers--not local failures.

The proposed state grant program fills this critical gap. It offers a practical, state-level solution where federal programs fall short. The per-student grant allows partnership sites to provide breakfast, lunch, and snacks without relying on federal reimbursement structures that do not align with mixeddelivery models. Infrastructure grants further address real-world challenges such as refrigeration, storage, and food preparation capacity.

Importantly, this program protects and strengthens public pre-K partnerships. Without sustainable meal funding, schools may hesitate to partner with community-based programs, limiting access to public pre-K--particularly in rural areas. This grant makes partnerships more viable, more equitable,

Testimony of Senator Henry Ingwersen supporting
LD 2064, An Act to Expand Access to Early Childhood Nutrition by Establishing a Grant Program for Public Preschools
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs Thursday, February 5, 2026
Good afternoon, Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and the esteemed Members of the Education and Cultural Affairs Committee. I am Senator Henry Ingwersen, and I proudly represent Senate District 32, which includes Arundel, Biddeford, Dayton, Hollis, and Lyman. Today, I offer testimony in strong support of President Daughtry's LD 2064, "An Act to Expand Access to Early Childhood Nutrition by Establishing a Grant Program for Public Preschools."
Last week, as the Senate chair of the Health and Human Services Committee, I was happy to work on two of my child care-related bills: LD 1728 and LD 2066.
The first bill, LD 1728, would put into Maine statute the federal child care subsidy rules that change the cap on co-payments for participants in the Child Care Affordability Program from 10% to 7%. It would allow the Health and Human Services Department to further reduce or waive these co-payments for families with a child with a disability, families experiencing homelessness and families with a foster child. The Department would have to post information related to co-payment amounts on its website. Finally, it would require the Department to issue subsidies based on enrollment, rather than attendance, encouraging more child care providers to participate in child subsidy programs without having to accept below-market rates for child care services.
The second bill, LD 2066, seeks to build on a successful two-year pilot program, which has demonstrated effective coordination with the Child Care Affordability Program. The bill would make the Child Care Employment Award a permanent component of Maine's child care subsidy system, along with the Child Care Affordability Program. As of September 2025, the program currently supports 511 Maine children from 313 working families. Without additional funding, 470 children from 312 families will remain on the waitlist.
While both of these bills invest in Maine's essential child care system and lower costs for working parents, they do not provide the full investment that our infants and toddlers deserve. President Daughtry's bill, LD 2064, recognizes that mixed delivery Pre-K is key for the survival
1

of the child care system as a whole. The lower ratio makes it profitable enough to uplift infant and toddler care.
It's also a direct response to persistent food insecurity in the state. Last fall, when the federal government shut down and withheld SNAP benefits, I spearheaded a letter to the U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins, which President Daughtry signed, urging the Secretary to tap into contingency funds and release SNAP benefits to the 170,000 Mainers - including children - who rely on this support.
At the same time, I met with community members at Youth Full Maine and the York County Food Pantry. I attended meetings with the Council of Mayors and the York County Food Council. But most importantly, during National School Lunch Week I served free school meals to students at Hollis School and Mildred L. Day School. While there, I spoke with District Nutrition Directors and nutrition staff, who assured me that the free school meal program is one of the most successful legislative efforts in recent state history. They report that more kids are eating school meals. This committee should feel proud that we were able to bring universal free school meals into law - and keep it there.
During the weeks of uncertainty surrounding SNAP, parents could breathe a little easier knowing their children would receive nutritious meals at school. Thinking back on that time now, it is clear to me that the state has to do more to take on food insecurity.
It's why I introduced LD 2004 this session. It seeks to open up the sources of funding of nutrition incentive programs, like Maine Harvest Bucks, so that the dollars are not dependent on federal match dollars. After all, if the federal dollars disappear, we cannot lose other sources of funding - allowing Mainers to go hungry.
With LD 2064, we can make a clear, strong commitment to feeding children when they are developing, growing, and learning. Aside from being the right thing to do, we cannot feed their minds unless we feed their bellies, too. And there are no do-overs: We either nurture children during these critical years or we miss the opportunity forever.
I thank the Committee for its time, and I urge all of you to vote Ought to Pass on LD 2064.
Henry Ingwersen State Senator, Senate District 32 Arundel, Biddeford, Dayton, Hollis, and Lyman

Re: Testimony in Support of LD 2064 - An Act to Expand Access to Early Childhood Nutrition by Establishing a Grant Program for Public Preschools
To: Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and Honorable Members of the Health and Human Services Committee
On behalf of the Maine Community Action Partnership (MeCAP) and the Community Action Agencies serving all sixteen counties, I write in strong support of LD 2064, An Act to Expand Access to Early Childhood Nutrition by Establishing a Grant Program for Public Preschools. This legislation is essential to ensuring that all children enrolled in public pre-K programs, regardless of setting or location, have equitable access to nutritious meals.
Currently, due to restrictions within federal child nutrition programs, community-based public pre-K classrooms are ineligible to participate in the universal school meal program. As a result, many providers operating outside school facilities face high costs to supply daily meals. LD 2064 addresses this critical gap by establishing a grant program that enables community-based programs to provide breakfast, lunch, and a snack for every enrolled child.
The bill also reinforces Maine's commitment to a mixeddelivery model for public pre-K by ensuring that community partners, who are essential to reaching rural areas and communities without schooladministered pre-K, have the resources needed to meet state standards. Without this support, providers are forced to absorb substantial mealrelated costs, which can lead to financial strain, reduced meal quality, and, ultimately, negative impacts on children and families who depend on these services.
Importantly, LD 2064 also establishes infrastructure grants to help programs build the capacity needed to prepare meals and manage nutrition services effectively. These supports are crucial for communitybased providers, who shoulder responsibility for meal preparation and distribution without access to the purchasing power or facilities available in schoolbased programs.
Passage of LD 2064 offers a practical, statelevel solution to a clearly identified federal funding gap and ensures that all Maine children in public pre-K have access to the highquality nutrition they need to learn and thrive. We respectfully urge the Committee to advance LD 2064 in support of equitable, highquality public pre-K for every child in Maine, regardless of income or geographic location.
Thank you for your consideration,
